speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: asked the Minister for Manpower in view of the findings that one in five resident workers are overqualified for their roles according to a study released on 14 April 2026 (a) what are the implications for underemployment among younger workers, women and lower-income groups; and (b) what preventative measures are in place to reduce persistent mismatch and strengthen skills utilisation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) how does the Ministry assess the impact of rising overqualification on (i) long-term career pathways and (ii) wage progression; and (b) what steps are being taken to enhance (i) job redesign, (ii) skills-based progression, and (iii) workforce readiness for future shifts in jobs and job scopes.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: That would be Question Nos 3 and 4?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Oral Question Nos 3 and 4, and also written questions filed by Ms Jessica Tan and Dr Wan Rizal for today's Sitting; and oral and written questions filed by Mr Yip Hon Weng1, Ms Cassandra Lee and Mr David Hoe2 for subsequent Sittings.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I would also like to invite Mr Yip, Ms Lee and Mr Hoe to seek clarifications today, and consider withdrawing their questions filed for future Sittings if their questions have been addressed.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This was below the high-income countries' average of 21.6%.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The remaining one in 10 of overqualified individuals were involuntarily overqualified.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As Ms Jessica Tan and Mr David Hoe noted, the voluntarily overqualified could include women and caregivers who may choose roles to explore a new career direction or to better fit around their family circumstances, even if they are overqualified for those roles.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To Dr Wan Rizal's question, involuntarily overqualified workers tend to be younger and tertiary-educated.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is consistent with typical early career pathways where workers may initially take on roles that do not fully utilise their qualifications before transitioning into better-matched roles as they gain experience.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The sector with the highest number of involuntarily overqualified workers was Transportation and Storage.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members are encouraged to refer to the Ministry of Manpower's (MOM's) Occasional Paper for more details.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Dr Wan Rizal and Ms Tan also asked about the impact of overqualification on longer-term career pathways.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: MOM currently does not track longitudinal outcomes of overqualified individuals.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We remain committed to help all individuals find jobs that can meet their personal needs as well as their career aspirations.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This includes helping lower-wage workers, which Ms Tan asked about, find the jobs that can better utilise their skills, as they may be in entry-level jobs that do not do so.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng, Ms Cassandra Lee and Ms Tan asked about our broader strategies to reduce skills mismatches.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At the pre-employment phase, the institutes of higher learning (IHLs) work closely with industry partners to equip students with industry-relevant technical competencies and skills.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And beyond initial qualifications, all of our workers are encouraged to, and they must, embrace lifelong learning.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The merger of Workforce Singapore (WSG) and SkillsFuture Singapore (SSG) into the Skills and Workforce Development Agency (SWDA) – later on today, I will be passing a Bill on that – will help our workers to do so by creating a single touchpoint for training, for career guidance and job opportunities.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I do hope that Members of the House will support the Bill unanimously.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: By bringing together the capabilities of both agencies, SWDA and its tripartite partners will be able to provide personalised career and skills insights and guidance to help jobseekers find options that better match their skills and their preferences.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Efforts by SWDA and the National Trades Union Congress' (NTUC's) Employment and Employability Institute will also build on existing upskilling and reskilling programmes that support our workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These include Career Conversion Programmes (CCPs), the Mid-Career Pathways Programme and the SkillsFuture Career Transition Programme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Female caregivers returning to work from a career break can also access career guidance and skills training through WSG's herCareer initiative.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To address diverse needs and working arrangement preferences, MOM and tripartite partners promote a range of work and career options.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This includes supporting enterprise job redesign for flexible work arrangements (FWAs) through the SkillsFuture Workforce Development Grant (Job Redesign+).

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Based on MOM's surveys, around 70% of firms offered FWAs in 2025, and this is up from 50% about six years earlier, in 2019.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I hear the Minister that we do not collect this data today, so I would like to ask how that goes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And I also like to build on the point about future workforce readiness, especially in terms of how we track skills utilisation and progression over time.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, if I could ask the Minister, what indicators do the Ministry use to determine if overqualification is becoming persistent rather than transitional and what thresholds would trigger further intervention?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: My second supplementary question is, does the Minister assess whether over qualification today may reduce readiness from emerging roles tomorrow and how is this risk being mitigated?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Because overqualifications can depress wage trajectories, weaken skills utilisation and reduce long-term workforce competitiveness.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We were able to derive these statistics using occupation and education data, which is captured from our annual labour workforce surveys, enabling us to determine whether a worker possesses educational qualifications that are higher than the typical requirements of a job.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Because up till now, based on even international published statistics, underemployment data typically use a time-related measure, and today, the time-related measure still remains the only internationally accepted statistical definition of underemployment and as a proxy, overqualification.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, we are starting, we will continue to monitor the trends over a longer time horizon.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will, first and foremost, of course, focus on more of the macroeconomic data pertaining to our gross domestic product (GDP) growth and also, our median wages.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With the different interventions across the different cohorts, segments and sectors, we would be able to, in time, track this data better and provide regular updates to this House.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We believe that, with the passage of time, we are also using – it is not a buzzword, but we are indeed using artificial intelligence at the different level of data analytics and triangulation, to allow us to work closely with our businesses and with the employers across different sectors, starting with those areas that we are more familiar with, to be able to better tweak and refine our policies to help our locals.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are starting here and we welcome ideas from Members of the House to help us to refine, improve and also to have better reach, more precise policies to reach out and uplift all of our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I also just want to highlight this to the Minister, that stepping out for caregiving should not mean stepping down permanently.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I hope the Minister can give assurance to caregivers that they will be able to assume back to their previous role, because many of these caregivers are parents with young children.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: How would MOM also assure youths that might not have many internships or less connected backgrounds, that they will not be significantly disadvantaged in a labour market that increasingly rewards early internship networks and overseas exposure, as reflected in The Straits Times article this morning?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Indeed, I think it is precisely why we are all coming together and to see how we can reach out to more caregivers, particularly should they choose the option of coming back to work.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think the Member would appreciate that the needs of caregivers are varied and they are also very, very complex.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I do not think there is a one-size-fit-all policy that would go in, flood the system and uplift everyone.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I do not think that any policy can do that.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If you just disburse in the form of a broad-based support, we may also end up not being able to get the desired outcome for those that need it the most.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, our approach has always been to work with different sectors, depending on the type of industry that the particular caregiver wants to come back into.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And I agree with the Member: stepping out does not mean stepping back or stepping down.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There will be plans to work according to the sectors, for them to have a refresh and upgrade of the skills, to retool, to reskill, so that they are ready should they choose to come back into the workforce.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For youth internship, I indeed take note of the article today written by Ms Lin Suling in The Straits Times, it was a very long opinion editoral.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But let me address one part which I think is important.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Today, the statistics that were cited in the article pertain to fresh graduate employment outcomes, which indeed have softened from recent peaks.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The peak was coming out from COVID-19, and everybody was rushing to fulfil backlog of orders, there was a big rush for graduates, for talent, coming on board.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But we should not be just looking at an isolated year-by-year number.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: What this tells us and the article is actually quite precise in talking about fresh graduates.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But I think it also demonstrates that some graduates may take longer to secure full-time roles initially.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And I take the Member's point with utmost importance, about the ability for our undergraduates to secure internships.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: What we are now actively doing is working – of course, this is before the SWDA is formed – we are actively working with our IHLs to bring attachments and exposure, with experienced volunteer career advisors, to build the networks for many of these young undergraduates while they are in-flight through our IHLs.
We hope to strengthen that programme even more.
We will continue to get these insights to see how we can work, particularly in sectors that are growth sectors that have a long runway, a long career trajectory, for our undergraduates.
We are going to emphasise the foremost importance of this in the next few months.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I just have a very short supplementary question, which is, what additional support, besides CCP and the SkillsFuture Career Transition Programme, is available for mid-career workers who may be persistently over-qualified in their roles, especially those who have undergone reskilling, but still remain mismatched.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some suggestions would include things like hand-holding, coaching and even case management for this group of workers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I do see a lot of them at my Meet-the-People Session.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Indeed, our jobs are evolving very quickly and companies are also having to keep up with that very rapid transformation of what is happening in the world economy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There is not a particular, single policy that we can introduce that would be a panacea to cover every single potential mid-career displacement.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On top of that, across different sectors, across different industries, when we get feedback, we will not hesitate to put up training programmes for those who want to seek a pivot or switch.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Monetary Authority of Singapore has a finance programme.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In the biopharma sector, we have a biopharma talent track programme that allows many of them to switch, and also, programmes in healthcare.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: They are varied, as long as we are able to encourage, to socialise the idea with our workforce that they are not discouraged, there will be something for everyone.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I can go on for the whole list of the different programmes that we have available, but I think it would probably be beyond the scope of this particular Parliamentary Question session.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But suffice to say that there are a lot of programmes out there.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Even for myself, holding many of the different portfolios and also with the different programmes that we have, when I want to search for something during my Meet-the-People Session, I also rely on ChatGPT to navigate my own Ministry's myriad of programmes that we have.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, I think you can envisage – it is actually a very comprehensive and a wide series of help that we have.
